posts.author: Cristiano_Perrucci
posts.content_md:
![Image](http://digilander.iol.it/crispers/hologram20x20.jpg)

Here is quite big and bright 20x20 (8x8 in) using a self made red sensitive MBDCG glass plate.

The formulation is the standard Jeff Blyth's with a few variation (TMG, MB and gelatine concentration, IPA baths temperature).

Exposure: 15' @ 20mW He-Ne laser with spatial filter installed.

Noise is surprisingly low although no post exposure hardening process was involved.

Cheers,

posts.author: Cristiano_Perrucci
posts.content_md:
> **dave battin:** very nice! do you still have the interferometer setup? this is the best ive seen yet, beautiful !Cristiano what was your coating method?

Dave,

no, of course! With a such long exposure time, a single photon makes the difference!! The Mitchelson interf. was promptly removed after the conference call with you and John.

The coating method for this plate was the "sandwich" described by Hans on the HoloWiki.

I would like to emphasize this method requires a few little adjustements:

- MB concentration SHOULD be tuned for optimum results depending of gelatine hardness and tape you are using (mine is 3.1 mils)

- Gelatine concentration MUST be tuned for differents kinds of gelatine and TMG concentration.

- During gelatine pouring, glass plates SHOULD be controlled for better results, and kept closely to emulsion temp.

- Traces of water repellent (I'm using Rain Clear as Rain X is unknown here in Italy) on glass surface helps to get a really smooth coating.

Finally I found that using boric acid instead of acetic acid, ALWAYS (3 attemps 3 failures) caused emulsion detaching from the glass during the first bath in cold water. I think this is caused by the gelatine I'm using (a premixed pig and bovine gel, ~280 bloom). But for a scientific explanation, it should be better ask Jeff...

I think this material is the best (and cheap) solution for the hobbist. Always works. As usual, thanks Jeff!

posts.author: Joe Farina
posts.content_md: That is a really stunning result, Cristiano, congratulations. It shows what is possible when someone has developed skill with MBDCG, using only a 20mW HeNe. And there should be no worries about mode-hopping with a HeNe of this power level (I have heard of some such problems when using the very large SP-125 with etalon). Considering the long exposures, were you using any special form of temperature control in your lab?

posts.author: Cristiano_Perrucci
posts.content_md:
> **Joe:** That is a really stunning result, Cristiano, congratulations. It shows what is possible when someone has developed skill with MBDCG, using only a 20mW HeNe. And there should be no worries about mode-hopping with a HeNe of this power level (I have heard of some such problems when using the very large SP-125 with etalon). Considering the long exposures, were you using any special form of temperature control in your lab?

Joe, the laser is a JDS-Uniphase 1145P bought on ebay for 103 USD, without power cable and power supply. The PSU is a simple 230V-1500V AC transformer followed by a voltage multiplier to get the ~4KV 6.5 mA required by the gas tube. This kind of Power Supply Unit is quite unstable and noisy, I really don't know if changes of biasing current might induce mode-hopping.

I don't have any kind of temperature control where I'm shooting my holograms, I just leave the laser on at least 3 hrs before exposing.

posts.author: Joe Farina
posts.content_md:
Thanks for the information and photos. The appearance of the hologram is even better in the second frontal photo, I guess your background is darker in that case.

As Michael mentioned, your setup must be very stable indeed if you're able to carry out 15 minute exposures and get that kind of fringe contrast. HeNe's are in no way immune to slow fringe drift, so yours must do very well in that respect also. (Perhaps a lesson can be learned from your 3 hour warmup period.) It's really inspiring to see someone make a DCG hologram like that with a $103 laser and an improvised power supply!

Your success raises a very intruiging question: can stability be refined to such a level that even longer exposures are possible? There are many papers discussing environmental stability for holography, but I wonder, is there still a lot to be learned? We all know that many factors affect table/component rigidity and long-term stability, and that the type of hologram geometry is also important (i.e, transmission or reflection, single-beam or split-beam, etc.). I am trying to implement some of the stabilty-enhancing techniques that I've learned as I build my lab.
